title: Charged for an order that cannot ship
question: An order flow reserves stock, charges the card, then books a courier. The courier service rejects the booking. The customer has been charged for an order that will never ship. What should the flow do?
context: Inventory, payments and shipping are separate services with their own databases. Each step commits on its own before the next begins.

options.label: Undo the finished steps in reverse — refund, then release the stock
options.why: Each step has already committed, so there is nothing to roll back; the way out is a compensating action per step, run in reverse order, each one idempotent so it can be retried. That is a saga. Ordering matters too: putting the step most likely to fail first would have avoided the charge.

options.label: Retry the courier booking every minute until it finally succeeds
options.why: Some failures are permanent — no courier covers the address, the parcel is too heavy — and a retry loop turns them into an order stuck forever with the customer's money. Retrying suits transient errors, not rejections.

options.label: Wrap the three service calls in one database transaction from the start
options.why: Each service has its own database, so no single transaction spans them. Making one would mean two-phase commit across services owned by different teams, holding locks while a courier API decides.

options.label: Leave it, and let support refund the customer when they complain
options.why: It turns a system failure into a customer's problem and a manual process that scales with the failure rate. The flow knows exactly what happened and what undoes it; it should do so itself.
